config.title: Conditional Rendering with Ternary

intro.title: Conditional Rendering with Ternary
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a dynamic Angular component that displays different content based on user state, such as showing a welcome message for logged-in users or a login prompt for guests. You'll learn conditional rendering, a fundamental programming concept that allows your application to display different UI elements based on data conditions. The lesson focuses on using the ternary operator (? :) within Angular templates to create clean, readable conditional logic directly in your HTML. You'll work with Angular's interpolation syntax, component properties, and template expressions to control what content appears on screen. By the end, you'll understand how to make your Angular applications respond dynamically to changing data and user interactions.
intro.usecase: Conditional rendering with ternary operators is essential for creating dynamic user interfaces that respond to user state and data conditions. You'll frequently use this pattern to show/hide loading spinners while API calls are in progress, display different content based on user authentication status (login forms vs. user dashboards), or toggle between edit and view modes in forms. E-commerce applications commonly use ternary operators to conditionally render 'Add to Cart' buttons for available items versus 'Out of Stock' messages, while social media platforms use them to show different post actions based on whether the current user owns the content. This pattern is also crucial for displaying error states, success messages, and empty state placeholders throughout modern web applications.

objectives: Implement ternary operators in Angular component templates to conditionally display content
Apply conditional logic to render different HTML elements based on component state
Construct template expressions that evaluate boolean conditions using ternary syntax
Configure component properties to control the visibility of UI elements
Manipulate DOM rendering by binding ternary expressions to element attributes
Initialize conditional display states in Angular components using TypeScript properties
Integrate ternary operators with Angular's interpolation syntax for dynamic content rendering

steps.title: Import Component decorator
steps.instruction: Import Component from @angular/core to set up the Angular component decorator needed for conditional rendering.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the Component decorator from Angular's core package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing a decorator
import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
steps.expectedOutcome: The Component decorator is imported and ready to be used for creating an Angular component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track with the import statement. Make sure you're importing Component from @angular/core.
steps.feedbackWrong: use the import statement to bring in Component from @angular/core. This decorator is needed to define Angular components.

steps.title: Create the main component class
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript class named ConditionalRenderingComponent and decorate it with @Component to define an Angular component.
steps.hint: Define a TypeScript class with the @Component decorator above it. The decorator should include selector and template properties.
steps.seedCode:
import { Component } from '@angular/core';

// Create the component class here
steps.expectedOutcome: A decorated TypeScript class that serves as an Angular component with selector and template configuration.
successCriteria: ConditionalRenderingComponent class is created and decorated with @Component decorator containing selector and template properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your class is decorated with @Component and includes both selector and template properties in the decorator configuration.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a TypeScript class named ConditionalRenderingComponent and add the @Component decorator above it with selector and template properties.

steps.title: Initialize boolean property for visibility
steps.instruction: Inside the component class, add a boolean property named 'isVisible' and set it to true.
steps.hint: In Angular components, properties are declared as class members. Add a line like 'isVisible = true;' inside the component class.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have a boolean property that can control conditional rendering
successCriteria: The component class contains a boolean property named 'isVisible' initialized to true
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure the property is named 'isVisible' and is set to a boolean value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The property should be a boolean named 'isVisible' inside the component class. Try adding 'isVisible = true;' as a class member.

steps.title: Define toggle method
steps.instruction: Create a method named toggleVisibility inside the ConditionalRenderingComponent class that toggles the isVisible property between true and false.
steps.hint: Define a method that changes this.isVisible to its opposite value using the logical NOT operator (!).
steps.expectedOutcome: A toggleVisibility method is added to the component class that switches the isVisible property between true and false.
successCriteria: The ConditionalRenderingComponent class contains a toggleVisibility method that toggles the isVisible property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your method toggles the isVisible property using the logical NOT operator.
steps.feedbackWrong: The method should be named toggleVisibility and should toggle the isVisible property between true and false.

steps.title: Create basic component template
steps.instruction: Add the @Component decorator above the class with a template property containing a div element with the text 'Conditional Rendering Demo'.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator with a template property. Inside the template, create a div with descriptive text about the demo.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class should have the @Component decorator with a template containing a div element.
successCriteria: @Component decorator is added with a template property containing a div with text content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start with the @Component decorator. Make sure the template property contains a div element with text content.
steps.feedbackWrong: add the @Component decorator above the class with a template property containing a div element.

steps.title: Add toggle button with click handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Toggle Visibility' that calls the toggleVisibility method when clicked using Angular event binding.
steps.hint: Use (click) event binding to connect the button to your toggleVisibility method. The syntax is (click)="methodName()".
steps.expectedOutcome: A button with 'Toggle Visibility' text that will call the toggleVisibility method when clicked.
successCriteria: Button element is added with (click) event binding that calls toggleVisibility method.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your button has the correct text and uses (click) event binding to call the toggleVisibility method.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button needs (click) event binding to connect to your toggleVisibility method. Use the syntax (click)="toggleVisibility()" on your button element.

steps.title: Add ternary conditional rendering
steps.instruction: Inside the template, below the button, add a paragraph that uses a ternary operator to conditionally display 'Content is visible!' when isVisible is true, or 'Content is hidden!' when isVisible is false.
steps.hint: Use the ternary operator syntax: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. Access the component property with 'isVisible'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Ternary operator example

{{ isLoggedIn ? 'Welcome back!' : 'Please log in' }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The template contains a paragraph that uses a ternary operator to show 'Content is visible!' when isVisible is true, or 'Content is hidden!' when isVisible is false.
successCriteria: A paragraph element uses the ternary operator with isVisible condition to display different messages for true and false states.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start with the ternary operator! Make sure you're checking the isVisible property and displaying the correct messages for both true and false conditions.
steps.feedbackWrong: use the ternary operator syntax: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. Check that you're using isVisible as the condition and showing appropriate messages for both cases.

steps.title: Add alternative content for false condition
steps.instruction: Update the existing ternary conditional to show 'Content is hidden' when isVisible is false, instead of showing nothing
steps.hint: Replace the 'null' in the false branch of the ternary with a paragraph element containing the text 'Content is hidden'

Show this

Show that instead
steps.expectedOutcome: The ternary conditional will show 'Content is visible!' when isVisible is true and 'Content is hidden' when isVisible is false
successCriteria: The ternary conditional displays 'Content is hidden' in the false branch instead of null
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure to replace the 'null' with 'Content is hidden' in the false branch of the ternary.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ternary conditional should show 'Content is hidden' when isVisible is false. Replace 'null' with the alternative text.
